name: Grace Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for doing this, Grace. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so feel free to tell me your public view and your private one. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead carpenter at Okoro Timber Structures. We build the big timber buildings: sports halls, church halls, a school canteen right now, using glulam, which is beams made by gluing layers of wood together so they can span thirty metres. I run two crews, about nine people, and my day starts at half six with the crane plan and the weather. If the wind's over a certain speed, we can't lift, so I'm on the weather app before I'm out of bed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's the hard part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the day the big beams go up and the building suddenly has a shape, like a ribcage. I use AI every day, to check the lift sequence, to draft method statements, to compare supplier prices, and I've got Mr. Okoro using it now too, which took some doing. The hard part is that he's 64 and wants to retire, and he's offered me a stake in the business, so my head is full of numbers most evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. That's not what I'd expect, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a very useful tool, just not the revolution people promised. I'd keep telling other tradespeople to use it for the boring paperwork. On my church's business network group I'd probably post something about practical uses, not hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd make my decision about the stake easier. If nothing radical changes, a good timber firm with a solid name is a safe thing to own. Daniel, my husband, is an accountant and he's already run the numbers twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy into the firm next year, probably a quarter share to start, using most of our savings plus a small business loan. I'd keep using AI to tighten up our quoting and planning. Over five years, I'd take over the running of it as Mr. Okoro steps back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, actually. It'd feel like the road ahead was clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would a quarter share cost, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Around eighty thousand, from what Mr. Okoro and Daniel have worked out. We've got about fifty saved between us, and the bank would do the rest. It's scary but it's the kind of scary I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the firm would be most affected by you taking over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Pete, the other senior carpenter. He's 48 and I think he expected it to be him. I'd want to keep him close and give him the jobs he's best at, because he's brilliant on the big lifts, he just hates paperwork and computers.

S0.say: AI is still very useful, just not the promised revolution. She'd keep urging tradespeople to use it for paperwork and post practical tips on her church business network.
S0.think: It would make buying into the firm easier, because a well-known timber firm is a safe thing to own if nothing radical changes. Her accountant husband Daniel has run the numbers twice.
S0.do: Buys a quarter share in the firm next year for about eighty thousand, using most of their savings and a business loan. Uses AI to sharpen quoting and planning and takes over the running of the firm over five years.
S0.feel: Calm and settled, with a clear road ahead.
S0.quote: It's scary but it's the kind of scary I like.
S0.fieldNote: Grace's situation is unusual: she's on the edge of becoming an owner, so every scenario is also a business decision. She's comfortable with technology and risk and is already the one teaching her boss. She thinks about a passed-over colleague with care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong change, not a revolution. That sounds like what I'm planning for already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good thing for firms that get ahead of it. Learn the tools, use them well, and you'll win more work. I'd say that to other small business owners, because a lot of them are scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me and for the firm, as long as I'm running it. We'd quote faster, plan better, waste less timber. The risk is the bigger firms getting it all first and undercutting us, so we'd need to move early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still buy the stake, maybe even sooner. I'd put money into some of the new kit, like a robotic total station for setting out and AI-based planning software, maybe twenty or thirty thousand over two years. I'd train both crews on it myself, starting with the ones who want to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy and excited, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about someone like Pete, who hates computers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep him on the tools and on the lifts, where he's the best I've got. Not everyone has to be on a tablet. I'd pair him with a younger guy who's good with the tech, so they cover each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lay anyone off if the tools let you do the same work with fewer people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather grow and take on more jobs with the same people. But if work dried up, I'd have to make hard choices, that's business. I'd want to be fair about it and help people find something else.

S1.say: The change is good for firms that get ahead of it, so learn the tools and win more work. She'd tell anxious small business owners exactly that.
S1.think: It's good for her and the firm if she's in charge: faster quotes, better planning, less waste. The risk is bigger firms adopting first and undercutting them.
S1.do: Buys the stake, perhaps sooner, and invests twenty to thirty thousand over two years in robotic setting-out tools and planning software. Trains both crews herself, starting with the willing.
S1.quote: Not everyone has to be on a tablet.
S1.fieldNote: Grace speaks as an owner-in-waiting, weighing competition and efficiency. Her free-market outlook shows in accepting hard choices as part of business, but she wants to be fair. Her plan for Pete is thoughtful and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Hm. That changes the maths on everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say it's going to be a hard few years and people need to look after each other, families, churches, businesses. I wouldn't call for big government schemes, but I'd want help aimed at getting people into new work. And I'd tell other firms to start adapting now, not next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think buying into the firm would be a big gamble in this one. If robots can put up a glulam frame as well as us, and big companies own the robots, a small firm like ours could be gone in a couple of years. I'd be putting our savings into something that might not exist in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on buying the stake, at least for the first year, and keep our savings liquid. I'd push Mr. Okoro to bring in robots and AI planning as fast as possible, so we're the ones using them and not the ones being undercut. And I'd try to get the firm into specialist work, like heritage timber and complex one-off buildings, where machines might take longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's the first one that really makes my stomach turn, mainly because of the money we'd be risking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on the stake. How would you explain that to Mr. Okoro?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd tell him straight. I'd say I still want it, but I'm not putting fifty thousand of our savings in until I see how fast this moves. He'd understand, he's careful with money too. He'd probably be quietly relieved to have more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your crews the week it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get them in the canteen, buy everyone breakfast, and tell them the truth: I don't know exactly what happens, but I'll keep them informed and I'll fight to keep the firm going. I'd also tell them to start learning whatever they can, because I can't promise anything beyond the next year.

S2.say: It will be a hard few years and families, churches and businesses need to look after each other. She wouldn't call for big government schemes but wants help aimed at getting people into new work, and urges firms to adapt now.
S2.think: Buying into the firm would be a big gamble, since big companies owning robots could wipe out a small timber firm within a couple of years. She'd be risking savings on something that might not exist in 2030.
S2.do: Holds off on buying the stake for at least a year and keeps savings liquid. Pushes the firm to adopt robots and AI planning fast and steers it toward specialist heritage and one-off work.
S2.feel: Anxious, mainly about the money she'd be risking.
S2.quote: I'd be putting our savings into something that might not exist in 2030.
S2.fieldNote: For Grace, the threat in this scenario is less about her own skills and more about the firm she's about to buy into. Her adaptability shows in pushing the firm to automate quickly. She'd be honest with her crews and admits she can't promise beyond a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to make the firm ready, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real window, and small businesses should use it to adapt rather than waiting for government to sort things out. Apprenticeships should start including robot work now. I'd say that in our trade association and to anyone at church who asks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to buy in, modernise the firm and make it the one the bigger contractors call when they need timber structures done with robots and people together. It's still a risk, but I think the risk of standing still is bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the quarter share in the first year and spend the next three getting the firm ready, robots for the heavy lifting and cutting, AI for planning and design. I'd send two of my best people on robotics courses at the firm's cost. By the time it arrived, I'd want us running a mixed crew, machines doing the repetitive work and people doing the judgement calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit nervous about the debt, but I'd feel like I was steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want people doing the judgement calls. Is that realistic, if AI can do almost anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not forever. But clients, especially churches and schools, will want a person they can shake hands with and blame if something goes wrong. I think that buys a firm like ours some years, not decades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change any plans you and Daniel have at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We were thinking of starting a family in two or three years. I'd probably keep to that, but I'd want the firm on solid ground first. Daniel would be the one keeping us sensible on the money side.

S3.say: Five years is a real window, and small businesses should adapt rather than wait for government. Apprenticeships should include robot work now, she'd say in her trade association and at church.
S3.think: Five years is enough to buy in, modernise and make the firm the one contractors call for mixed robot and human timber work. Standing still is the bigger risk.
S3.do: Buys the quarter share in year one and spends three years adding robots for lifting and cutting and AI for planning. Sends two top workers on robotics courses at the firm's cost and aims for mixed crews when AGI arrives.
S3.feel: Mostly calm, a little nervous about the debt, but feeling in control.
S3.quote: Clients, especially churches and schools, will want a person they can shake hands with and blame if something goes wrong.
S3.fieldNote: Five years flips the stake decision back to yes, and Grace becomes confident again. Her view that human value lies in trust and accountability is honest about its limits. Family plans stay on track, with her husband as the money check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37, running the firm, hopefully with kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for any firm or family to get ready, and the ones who don't have only themselves to blame. Keep apprenticeships strong, adapt the business, look after your people. That's my message.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel very good about it. Ten years is enough to take over the firm fully, pay off the loan and bring in robots at the right pace. I'd still think about what happens to people like Pete, but I'd have time to find him a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy the stake next year as planned and take over the firm over five years. Bring in robots once they're proven on a few big sites, around year four or five, rather than paying for the first generation. Start a family with Daniel around thirty, like we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even. It feels like the kind of change I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who don't get ready have only themselves to blame. Would you say that to Pete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not like that. I'd say it more gently. Pete's different, he's given thirty years to the trade, and I'd make sure he's looked after, maybe as a site trainer or on the specialist jobs. I suppose I'm harder in general than I am with people I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the firm to look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe twelve people instead of nine, half the heavy work done by machines, and still the firm churches call when they want a hall that'll last a hundred years. And Mr. Okoro's name still on the van. I'd keep that.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for any firm or family to prepare, and those who don't have only themselves to blame. Keep apprenticeships strong, adapt the business and look after your people.
S4.think: She'd feel very good, with time to take over the firm, pay off the loan and bring in robots at the right pace. She'd still think about Pete but would have time to find him a place.
S4.do: Buys the stake next year as planned and takes over the firm over five years. Brings in robots around year four or five once proven, and starts a family with Daniel around thirty.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, a change she can plan for.
S4.quote: And Mr. Okoro's name still on the van. I'd keep that.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Grace sees AGI almost as an opportunity to grow the firm. When challenged, she admits she's harder in general than with people she knows, which is an honest moment. Loyalty to her old boss's name shows her traditional streak alongside her ambition.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits just as I'm about to put our savings into the firm. What would help is cheap loans or tax breaks for small firms to buy robots, so it's not only the giant companies who own them, and apprenticeship funding that covers robot work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who owns the machines. If it's only the biggest firms, then towns lose their local builders. If small firms can own them too, then maybe we keep something of what we have now.

headlineQuote: I suppose I'm harder in general than I am with people I know.
portrait: Grace Patel is a 27-year-old lead carpenter at a firm that builds large glulam timber halls, a daily AI user who has even got her 64-year-old boss using it, and who is weighing an offer to buy a stake in the business. She is calm in the AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, where she'd buy in and invest in new equipment. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious, mainly because of the savings she and her husband Daniel would risk, so she'd delay the stake and push the firm to automate fast. With five or ten years she buys in, brings robots in at a sensible pace and keeps her family plans.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would hit just as she was about to put their savings into the firm.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans or tax breaks so small firms can buy robots too, and apprenticeship funding that covers robot work.
